That is why safeguards must operate before appointments...” “No government should be allowed to turn a temporary parliamentary majority into enduring influence over the courts.” The 22nd Amendment would raise the Court of Appeal ceiling from 20 to 25 judges, including its President. The Judicature Amendment Bill would raise the High Court ceiling from 110 to 120. Adding previously recorded vacancies gives the following calculation. The constitutional danger is not the appointment of 40 judges as such. The danger arises when a large number of judicial positions are created or filled within an exceptionally short period and the appointments are concentrated in the hands of the President. Such a process can alter the composition of the judiciary for many years and may create the functional equivalent of court packing, even if each individual appointment is formally lawful. The Government should not proceed with judicial expansion until it explains how the additional judges will be selected, why these numbers are necessary and what prevents political preference from shaping the bench. The central question is whether the manner, timing, scale and selection mechanism of approximately 40 appointments could allow the political executive to reshape the judiciary within a short period. That danger a politically controlled restructuring of the courts is the risk Parliament must confront. BASL concerns over High Court and Court of Appeal Appointments The Bar Association of Sri Lanka’s concern goes directly to the appointment process. In a letter to the President reported on 31 December 2025, BASL questioned departures from seniority in promotions involving judicial officers and judges of the High Court and Court of Appeal. BASL called for transparent, fair appointments and promotions. It urged that seniority remain the basis for promotion until objective, defensible merit guidelines existed, subject to recognised demerit or other objectively identifiable compelling circumstances. That warning exposes a fundamental accountability problem. If merit justifies passing over a candidate, the standards for judging merit must be known. Otherwise, the public cannot distinguish professional assessment from preference. The answer must be a published procedure that can be applied consistently, not an assurance that the right people will be chosen. The IMF identified the same institutional weakness The IMF’s 2023 Governance Diagnostic Assessment separately identified an absence of clear, transparent procedures for senior judicial selection. Paragraph 285 of the assessment also reported no documented criteria supporting judicial promotion, transfer and career progression, while noting extensive responsibilities concentrated within a small JSC structure. This finding predates the present administration. It identifies an inherited vulnerability that the Government has a responsibility to address before expanding appointments. The IMF recommended clearer criteria for recruitment, promotion and dismissal, alongside protection for institutional independence. The 2025 IMF review also noted plans to collate and review existing judicial conduct guidance furthermore. The Speaker shut the door on scrutiny The transparency controversy had already reached Parliament. On 21st November 2025, Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa, myself, and several other Members of Parliament submitted a motion for a select committee to examine the JSC’s exercise of appointment, promotion, transfer, dismissal and disciplinary powers.The proposed inquiry asked whether decisions followed the Constitution and relevant rules, whether reasons were recorded and communicated, and whether extraneous considerations had influenced decisions. On 9 January 2026, Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne ruled the motion out of order. He said parliamentary oversight of JSC operations would violate the constitutional separation of powers and judicial independence. The motion therefore preceded the BASL letter reported in December; its rejection followed that warning. In my view, however, the Speaker’s decision to rule the motion out of order was wrong. Judicial independence should not place the Judicial Service Commission beyond legitimate parliamentary scrutiny. Article 4(c) of the Constitution itself provides that the judicial power of the People shall be exercised by Parliament through courts, tribunals and institutions created or recognised by the Constitution or by law. Scrutiny is not interference. If Parliament, which derives its authority from the sovereignty of the People, cannot question the transparency and accountability of the JSC, then who can? Judicial independence must protect the judiciary from improper influence, not shield the institutions governing it from legitimate questions of accountability. The court packing risk posed by the proposed 22nd Amendment must be understood against this background: an expansion of judicial appointments while questions about the transparency of selection remain unresolved and parliamentary scrutiny has been rejected. Vacancies Cannot Become a Political Opportunity My considered view is that vacancies were allowed to accumulate so appointments could later be made in bulk. The figures alone cannot prove that motive. However, the President’s reference to the Easter Sunday High Court Trial and promotion consequences does not, in my view, justify the delays. The four reported Supreme Court vacancies separately require a clear explanation: when did they arise, what prevented appointments and why did the delays continue? The consequences are already visible. Justice Dhammika Ganepola retired on 8 May 2026 without elevation to the Supreme Court despite four vacancies, a concern expressly raised by BASL. Justice Rathanapriya Gurusinghe also retired without elevation despite a recommendation from former Chief Justice Murdu Fernando, according to BASL’s President. Experienced judges thus retired while opportunities for appointment remained. In my view, this sequence deepens the suspicion of an ulterior motive and demands a direct answer from the President. A concentrated wave of appointments can shape the courts for years, even where each appointment satisfies formal requirements. Delays in filling judicial vacancies must not become a political opportunity to reshape the judiciary through appointments made in bulk. Judicial independence belongs to the institution Judicial independence is not merely the independence of individual judges; it is also the institutional independence of the judiciary from the political branches of government. A government need not instruct a judge how to decide a case to threaten that independence. Political influence over the selection process can affect the institutional balance before a case is heard. That is why safeguards must operate before appointments, rather than depend on proving interference afterwards. Court packing has a global playbook Venezuela shows how expansion can become capture Venezuela supplies a particularly relevant warning. In 2004, legislation expanded its Supreme Court from 20 to 32 members. Human Rights Watch reported that the governing coalition filled the 12 new seats and 5 existing vacancies, describing the process as court packing. The lesson for Sri Lanka concerns that combination. New seats, accumulated vacancies and politically influenced selection can enable a rapid restructuring. The comparison is about the danger of that mechanism; it does not establish that Sri Lanka has already reproduced Venezuela’s outcome. Argentina and Roosevelt reveal the same temptation In Argentina, President Carlos Menem expanded the Supreme Court from 5 to 9 members in 1990. Human Rights Watch records that allies filled the new openings, producing what became known as an “automatic majority”. Court size became an instrument of political advantage. Roosevelt’s 1937 proposal could have expanded the US Supreme Court from 9 justices to 15 after the Court struck down major New Deal measures. The expansion failed in Congress. It remains a warning that administrative explanations can accompany attempts to change judicial composition. Poland: Changing Who Chooses the Judges Poland’s 2017 reforms shifted the selection of 15 judicial members of the National Council of the Judiciary to Parliament, created new Supreme Court chambers and lowered the retirement age. The Venice Commission warned that approximately 40% of Supreme Court judges could leave, with replacements appointed through a newly constituted council dominated by political appointees. Hungary: Clearing Seats, Controlling Succession Hungary’s 2012 changes abruptly reduced judges’ mandatory retirement age from 70 to 62. The Venice Commission estimated that between 225 and 270 judges, including many senior officeholders, would retire within a short period. It found no convincing justification for forcing out a generation of serving judges. A six month moratorium on judicial appointments compounded the concern. The Commission considered that this appeared intended to channel new appointments including court leadership positions through the new system, giving the newly elected President of the National Judicial Office a central role. Hungary therefore illustrates why the timing of vacancies and the arrangements for filling them deserve scrutiny alongside changes to court numbers. Explain the Expansion Before Approving It The Government must explain why five additional Court of Appeal judges and ten additional High Court judges are necessary, and how those numbers were determined. Parliament and the public are entitled to see the workload figures, vacancy records and reasons supporting the proposed increases. BASL’s concerns and the IMF’s findings make transparency in appointments particularly urgent. The Government should explain how it proposes to address those concerns, while respecting the distinct constitutional responsibilities of the President, the Judicial Service Commission and the Constitutional Council. Parliament should not approve an expansion of judicial appointments while fundamental questions about their necessity and the transparency of selection remain unanswered. The Government’s Term Will End. Its Appointments Will Remain. BASL has called for transparency. The IMF has identified weaknesses in judicial selection. The proposed parliamentary inquiry has been rejected. Against that background, expanding the opportunities for appointment before addressing the safeguards is a constitutional risk the country should not accept. The Government must publish the justification for expansion, account for the accumulated vacancies and establish clear selection criteria. Parliament should insist on those answers before approving additional seats. The public is entitled to know how those entrusted with administering justice are chosen. A concentrated wave of appointments can shape the judiciary long after this Government leaves office. By the time the consequences become clear, the opportunity to prevent them may have passed. No government should be allowed to turn a temporary parliamentary majority into enduring influence over the courts. The judiciary must remain strong enough to hold accountable the very people who appoint its judges. The former Secretary of State shared this message on his social media account on X, referencing the report titled «Hungarian Justice Pursues Miklós Szánthó for Fraud, a Key Link for Kast in the International Far-Right Agenda» , developed by the El Ciudadano Investigation Team . Jackson emphasized the need for clarification of the case , as well as the modus operandi and influence of this network associated with the current head of state. « I hope everything is investigated to trace every branch of this international far-right network ,» he wrote. Esto pinta muy mal para el círculo de Orbán, uno de los socios internacionales del Pdte Kast. Ojalá se investigue todo para llegar hasta cada una de las ramificaciones de esta red internacional de ultraderecha. https://t.co/nAiVYUnqVX — Giorgio Jackson (@GiorgioJackson) October 2, 2026 The Prime Minister’s Office lodged a complaint after reviewing state grants awarded between 2021 and 2024 to Jogállam és Igazság Nonprofit Kft., the entity managing the Center for Fundamental Rights (Alapjogokért Központ), led by Miklós Szánthó. The goal is to determine whether budget fraud and mismanagement occurred regarding the allocation of 410 million forints. The filing does not imply that Szánthó has been formally accused or convicted; it is now up to the authorities to assess whether a crime took place and who might be responsible. The review uncovered 188.5 million forints (approximately 576 thousand dollars) in fees for the three main leaders: Szánthó, Gergely István Kovács, and Péter Törcsi. Each is said to have received 1,431,639 forints monthly , a figure that increased to 1,574,803 forints in June 2023. According to the Government, there is no record of external approval or oversight of these salary decisions. These fees account for 46% of the 410 million forints under investigation, marking a significant irregularity in the case. Notably, a 2023 agreement shows Miklós Szánthó signing for both parties , acting as both contractor and contracted. Additionally, beneficiaries were required to submit professional reports on project execution, but the submitted documents were described as «general» and, according to the Government, did not include studies or research substantiating specific funded activities. Recorded activities include press conferences, radio and television interviews, and web content. The central question of the investigation is: « What products were actually delivered in exchange for the 410 million forints of public funds? « Connection Between Miklós Szánthó and José Antonio Kast Miklós Szánthó is not an ordinary leader; he heads the Center for Fundamental Rights, one of the central think tanks of Viktor Orbán’s government, and has turned Hungary into a hub for international far-right coordination . He is among the figures behind CPAC Hungary , a platform that gathers leaders, parliamentarians, and national-conservative organizations from Europe, the United States, and Latin America. His connection to José Antonio Kast has been documented. The Center for Fundamental Rights is part of the international network tied to the Political Network for Values (PNfV) , an organization that was presided over by Kast from March 2022 to 2024 . Documents obtained by El Mostrador confirm that the PNfV received over 405 million forints from Orbán’s Government between 2020 and 2024, including a disbursement of 355.4 million forints in 2022 , the year Kast assumed the presidency. In 2022, the PNfV hosted CPAC Hungary , held under the auspices of the Center led by Szánthó. In March 2026, Szánthó participated in Santiago at the conference titled «Freedom and Patriotism: A New Era on Both Sides of the Atlantic,» held a day before the inauguration of the far-right leader. On this occasion, he stated: «Common sense prevailed in Chile with Kast’s victory» , who in turn thanked Orbán «for his generosity in sharing his experiences and methods that have worked for them.» «We need people who can show the way,» he emphasized. As highlighted in the El Ciudadano report , the investigation has only just begun and will need to cross-check documents and determine responsibilities in what constitutes the internationalization of the Orbán model with Hungarian state funds. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Limoges city hall was destroyed over a weekend of protests and riots. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images First Edition newsletter France Monday briefing: What you need to know about a weekend of chaos in France In today’s newsletter: Violent riots and looting have dominated the headlines, but the unrest gripping the country and beyond reflects deeper public anger over everyday issues Hettie O'Brien Mon 19 Oct 2026 01.45 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. I bet your weekend was better than Emmanuel Macron’s. On Friday, the evening before mass protests that were planned across France, he attended a Céline Dion concert in Paris with his wife, Brigitte, prompting comparisons to Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette. On Sunday evening, he was forced to give a televised speech condemning the “unbridled violence” and riots that erupted in French cities over the weekend. The rioters that burned makeshift barricades of bicycles in Paris, destroyed the steeple of Limoges’ town hall and set fire to Lyon’s tourism office were described as “LE CHAOS” on the front page of La Tribune Dimanche, and “SCENES D’INSURRECTION” on Le Parisien Dimanche. By Sunday, protests had also taken place in Spain, Portugal and Italy. Today’s newsletter explains what happened in France over the weekend, and why this crisis threatens to engulf Macron’s government. First, here are the weekend’s headlines. Weekend roundup The Vatican | Pope Leo told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square on Sunday that he would “gradually resume” his activities, at his first appearance before the faithful since undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung. UK news | A “well-known individual” is trying to secure a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to prevent them from publishing details of serious allegations made against him. US politics | Donald Trump fired his immediately embattled new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, on Friday evening after just five days in the job. The conservative commentator becomes the shortest serving occupant of the role in US history. Reform | A Reform UK mayor is under police investigation for allegedly showing “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff. Luke Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion, is understood to have been questioned under caution by Humberside police. Energy | The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback after Microsoft pulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies. In depth: ‘Gen Z is really facing a polycrisis of different issues’ View image in fullscreen Most of the protests were peaceful marches calling for change. Photograph: Geoffroy van der Hasselt/AFP/Getty Images In the early hours of Sunday, cleaners started to remove the detritus from Parisian streets: shards of glass from broken shop windows, smashed bus shelters, burned out cars. The smell of teargas still lingered in the Métro station at Place de la République. “Areas of Paris looked like a wasteland,” Paolo Stuppia , a sociologist at Sciences Po in Paris, tells me. About 855 people have been arrested in Paris, and a total of 2,400 have been arrested across France. Lamia El Aaraje, the Socialist deputy mayor of Paris, said the capital had experienced a level of violence “we had never seen before.” There have been so many incredible images of destruction (see our gallery here ) that it’s possible to forget Saturday was, for the most part, defined by peaceful protests. Hundreds of thousands of people, many of them schoolchildren and parents, joined marches across the country. A far smaller group of protesters, many wearing face masks, smashed street furniture and torched cars and bus stops. A third group took the opportunity to loot shops. “I saw teenagers running off with shoeboxes, clothes, and perfume,” Angelique Chrisafis , the Guardian’s Paris correspondent, tells me. It’s the second group that has dominated the headlines. On Saturday afternoon, people set the town hall in Limoges alight (its spire collapsed dramatically on Saturday evening), and broke into the city hall in Marseille. “It wasn’t as if the peaceful protesters suddenly turned violent,” Chrisafis says. “It was as if the government didn’t have a hold on the situation, and suddenly, the police were really caught off guard.” The peaceful protesters ‘Our future is being stolen from us’ When a small number of people break the law during otherwise peaceful protests, there’s a tendency to condemn such acts as “criminality, pure and simple” (to quote David Cameron during the 2011 London riots), and to disqualify the idea they represent a form of antagonism against authority. “If everything was going well in France, you wouldn’t have young kids ransacking stores,” Stuppia says. Such criminal acts can also become a means of undermining peaceful protesters. “Some of those people are now pretty upset because they believe the government will be talking about burning barricades rather than the fact they turned out in such large numbers,” Chrisafis says. French students have been protesting against the school system since September and calling for repairs to decrepit buildings, smaller class sizes, and reforms to a widely loathed university admissions system. Education is a particularly fraught subject in France, where academic credentials overwhelmingly determine job prospects. But their concerns are also broader; as Greta Thunberg put it recently, “our future is being stolen from us,” a feeling that many young people across the continent share. The student protests have since become the focus in a constellation of different issues, ranging from the cost of living to rising fuel prices and public service cuts. Those on Saturday drew in numerous groups, including unions and supporters of the Gilets Jaunes. “Gen-Z is really facing a polycrisis of different issues, from the climate crisis to the rise of the far right and the use of AI” Stuppia tells me. “And you can see the same set of issues coming alive in Italy, in Belgium, in Portugal, and with the Cockroach protests in India. Young people want change.” (You can read more about how these protests have spread to other European countries in this story by Sam Jones ). The police ‘Entire cities … left to the mercy of rioters’ The police response has been at once strikingly brutal and remarkably inept. As Guardian columnist Rokhaya Diallo pointed out in this recent opinion piece , French schoolchildren have been “treated like enemies to be crushed” over the last few weeks. French lawyers have said that several teenagers have suffered “war-like” injuries from police, including a 14-year-old boy who suffered a fractured jaw and a 15-year-old whose hand was blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. The number of arrests has also been disproportionate: according to this graph by Pierre Bataille, a sociologist at Grenoble Alpes university, more people were arrested during two weeks of the student protests than members of the Gilets Jaunes were in an entire year. The shortcomings of this zealous focus on student protesters became clear on Saturday afternoon. Crowd psychologists have demonstrated that rather than instilling order, heavy-handed policing can actually trigger violence. While the police blocked a demonstration route between Place de la République and Place de la Concorde on Saturday citing “serious risks of public disorder,” large sections of Paris were left without enough officers to prevent looting. According to the French Green leader Marine Tondelier, “entire cities were left to the mercy of rioters, while peaceful protesters were subjected to violence.” She has since been calling for the resignation of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, calling his performance over the weekend “an absolute disaster”. The politicians ‘Social unrest is shaking our country’ In his statement last night , Macron drew a distinction between protesters with “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed, and looted”, and criticised “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents” (pending an investigation, though, it’s impossible to say what the rioters’ motivations were). There are tricky and enduring questions that his government now faces. It failed to anticipate both the student protests that have engulfed France since September, and the violence that broke out over the weekend. As this interesting New Yorker piece (£) points out Macron’s experience of the public education system is limited, and even his education minister has admitted that at least some of his five children attend private schools. The protests and the police response have underscored how out of touch Macron’s government appears to be with French people, many of whom are angry about the price of fuel and the cost of living. This sense of disaster – described by the mayor of Limoges, Guillaume Guérin, a member of the conservative Les Républicains party, as a “colossal failure of the state” – has overshadowed the thousands of people who turned out for peaceful protests, and plays into the hands of the far right (Marine Le Pen, who gave her own address on X before Macron’s, has described the riots as a “threat to democracy”). In a recent interview with Le Monde, the mayor of Lyon, Grégory Doucet, struck a more dispassionate tone, and said there need to be “concrete, political answers” to “the social unrest shaking our country.” The week to come Monday | The two-week biodiversity summit, Cop17, begins in Yerevan, Armenia, as countries come together to seek to protect nature. Tuesday | The Covid-19 inquiry publishes its report on the adult social care sector. Sunday | Incumbent Lula da Silva takes on Flavio Bolsonaro in the run-off of the Brazil general election. Photograph: David Levenson/Getty Images A spy charge, a Russian jail and a swap for an assassin: the story of Evan Gershkovich US journalist Evan Gershkovich talks to Annie Kelly about his arrest by the Russian intelligence services in 2023, his 16-month detention, and the swap deal that eventually took him home . Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld View image in fullscreen Illustration: Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Threats to the puffin population can be mitigated. Photograph: Tim Graham/Alamy In this extract from his book The Puffin, Stephen Moss explains how for centuries, humans exploited puffins for food and ​feathers, but they have since become beloved symbols of wildlife . Sadly just as our national affection for them has grown, ​w​e are now endangering their future. Pollution and climate change are disrupting marine ecosystems, reducing key prey and making it harder for puffins to raise chicks. But there are reasons to be hopeful that we can turn the tide. Restricting industrial fishing, removing invasive predators and using advanced tracking technology can help us understand and therefore protect the humble puffin. As Moss says: “perhaps we can maintain at least a small fragment of hope for the future not just of the puffin, but of all the world’s seabirds.​” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? https://www.dw.com/en/what-to-know-about.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5P9Qy Prefer DW on Google The Women's Ice Hockey World Championship is being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to 16 Image: Tomi Hänninen/Newspix24/IMAGO Advertisement Why is the tournament being held in November? Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time. The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL) , widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December. "This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating." How has the tournament format changed? Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception. Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament. Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark Will Russia be competing at this tournament? No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City. Who are the contenders? As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February. Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland , the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland , who took bronze in Milan. Why are the US and Canada not wearing their traditional uniforms? The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute. The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem. "While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada said.
